reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Presents with shoulder pain, weakness on elevation and abduction, and difficulty with overhead activities; supraspinatus is the most commonly torn tendon
Tears may be degenerative (attritional, in older patients) or traumatic (e.g. after a fall or dislocation, especially in those over 40)
A painful mid-range arc of abduction and positive cuff tests (e.g. weakness of resisted abduction or external rotation, drop-arm sign) support the diagnosis
Ultrasound and MRI are the key investigations, distinguishing partial from full-thickness tears and assessing tendon retraction and muscle atrophy
Many degenerative partial or small full-thickness tears are managed conservatively with physiotherapy, activity modification, and analgesia

Acute traumatic tears in younger, active patients and large tears with functional loss are generally considered for surgical repair, ideally before significant retraction and fatty muscle degeneration
Chronic massive, irreparable tears may lead to cuff-tear arthropathy, sometimes treated with reverse shoulder arthroplasty
New weakness after shoulder dislocation in an older patient should prompt assessment for an acute cuff tear, not just presumed axillary nerve injury
reference.pathophysiology: The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis) stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid and enables elevation and rotation. Tendon integrity is compromised by age-related degeneration, hypovascularity near the supraspinatus insertion, and mechanical impingement beneath the coracoacromial arch, making tears increasingly common with age. Repetitive overhead loading and acute trauma superimpose on this degeneration. Once a tear occurs, the tendon tends to retract and the corresponding muscle undergoes atrophy and fatty infiltration over time, reducing repairability and allowing superior migration of the humeral head, which can eventually produce cuff-tear arthropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Subacromial impingement or bursitis without tear
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the shoulder to assess cuff integrity dynamically
MRI to characterise tear size, retraction, and muscle quality (fatty atrophy)
Plain radiographs to assess acromial morphology, humeral head position, and arthropathy
Clinical cuff-specific strength tests (e.g. empty-can, external rotation, lift-off, drop-arm)
MR arthrography where partial or labral lesions are suspected
redFlags: Acute loss of active shoulder movement after trauma or dislocation suggesting an acute repairable tear
Weakness that could reflect nerve injury (axillary or suprascapular) requiring differentiation from cuff rupture
Signs of infection in a hot, swollen, systemically unwell shoulder
Progressive functional loss and pseudoparalysis indicating a large or massive tear
reference.prognosis: Many small and degenerative tears remain functionally acceptable with rehabilitation, but larger or acute traumatic tears repaired promptly generally do better than chronic retracted tears with fatty muscle degeneration; untreated massive tears can progress to cuff-tear arthropathy with persistent weakness and pain.
pitfalls: Assuming all post-dislocation weakness in older patients is axillary nerve palsy and missing an acute cuff tear
Delaying repair of an acute traumatic tear until retraction and fatty atrophy make it irreparable
Relying on radiographs alone, which do not show the tendon
Confusing frozen shoulder with a cuff tear by not distinguishing passive from active range restriction
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
